segments.narration: Iron Age islanders built a wall around a meteorite crater. Kaali, on Saaremaa, off the coast of Estonia.
The main crater is 110 metres wide and 22 metres deep, now filled with water. Eight smaller ones lie within a kilometre.
The rock came in at up to 20 kilometres a second and broke apart in the air. The blast was close to a small nuclear bomb.
And people were living there when it hit, though nobody agrees when that was, with estimates running from about 7,600 to 3,000 years ago. So what do you build after the sky explodes?
A 470-metre stone wall around the lake, with animal bones heaped inside, horses, sheep, oxen. Estonians called it the holy lake.

verdicts.claim: At Kaali on Saaremaa, Estonia, a stone wall was built around the main meteorite crater lake in the early Iron Age.
verdicts.note: 93% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: The main Kaali crater is 110 metres in diameter and 22 metres deep and holds a lake, with eight smaller craters 12 to 40 metres across lying within one kilometre.
verdicts.note: 75% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 4 number(s)

verdicts.claim: The Kaali meteoroid struck at an estimated 10 to 20 kilometres per second, broke up at 5 to 10 kilometres altitude, and released about 80 terajoules, roughly 20 kilotons of TNT.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia gives an estimated impact speed of 10 to 20 km/s, break-up at 5 to 10 km altitude, and impact energy of about 80 TJ or about 20 kilotons of TNT, which it compares to the Hiroshima bomb. The narration's 'close to a small nuclear bomb' is that comparison.

verdicts.claim: The area was populated at the time of impact, but published estimates of when it happened range from about 7,600 to about 3,000 years ago.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia says the site was populated when the impact occurred and records estimates spanning roughly 7,600 years ago to the 4th century BC, with the most recent put shortly after 1530 to 1450 BC. The EGU2015-3053 abstract gives radiocarbon ages of 1800 to 1500 BC and argues these may underestimate the age, while the Moora et al. abstract favours about 7600 radiocarbon years BP. Because the sources genuinely disagree the narration gives the range and states that nobody agrees rather than naming a date.

verdicts.claim: The early Iron Age wall around the Kaali lake was about 470 metres long and the bones of horses, sheep, oxen and other domestic animals were found inside it, and the lake was regarded as sacred.
verdicts.note: 95% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 1 number(s)
